unit.title: Assemble & disassemble scaffolding to enable access to the work area

summary: This unit teaches you to plan safe access for electrical work at height, and to assemble, inspect, use and dismantle mobile towers and small access scaffolds under trained supervision. You will learn the parts of a scaffold, how a tower is built in the maker's order with guardrails fitted from a safe position, how a scaffold is inspected and tagged, how people below are protected, the special electrical dangers of metal scaffolds, and how to lead a team on a job at height.

blocks.p: Electricians work at height every week: lights and fans on high ceilings, cable tray along warehouse walls, floodlights, security cameras, conduit above shop floors. Falls from height are among the most common causes of death at work, and most of them come from short jobs done from the wrong equipment. This unit is for Level 3 trainees who choose the access for a job, lead a team that builds and uses a mobile tower or a small scaffold, and make sure it is inspected, used and taken down safely. Scaffolds are built only by trained, authorised people; at the Centre that is the instructor, with trainees working under direct supervision.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan access
Survey the floor, height, space, people and hazards; choose between ladder, podium, tower, fixed scaffold and powered platform; write the risk assessment and method statement.
Know the equipment
Name the parts of a tube-and-fitting scaffold and a mobile tower and say what each does; check parts before use.
Assemble
Build a tower in the maker's order, level, with castors locked and outriggers fitted, and with guardrails put in from a safe position at every level.
Inspect and tag
Carry out a check before use with a checklist; understand the tag system and the inspections a competent person must make.
Use safely
Keep to the safe working load, climb inside, never move an occupied tower, protect people below and tie off tools.
Control electrical hazards
Keep metal scaffolds clear of overhead lines, isolate before work near boards and busbars, and find hidden cables before drilling.
Deal with weather and ground
Check the base after rain, stop for wind, and secure or dismantle before a storm.
Use fall protection
Know when a harness is required, check it, clip to a proper anchor and have a rescue plan.
Dismantle and store
Take the scaffold down top first, lower parts by hand, check and sort parts, quarantine damaged ones and store them under cover.
Lead the team
Check training, brief the team, supervise erection and use, keep records and report damage.

blocks.note: Jamaican health and safety law places duties on employers and workers to make work at height safe, and the Centre's and sites' own rules say who may erect scaffolds. Where a rule is not spelled out, Jamaican sites usually follow the practice of OSHA (US) or the British HSE. This kit uses those practices; follow your instructor and the site rules where they differ.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Working at height** means any work where a person could fall a distance that could injure them: from a platform, a ladder, a roof edge, or beside an open pit. There is no 'safe' height. The order of control is: avoid the work at height where you can (for example, lower a fitting on a winch to be serviced); if you cannot, prevent falls with guarded platforms; if a fall is still possible, limit its effect with a harness and a rescue plan.

ul: **The floor or ground**: firm or soft, level or sloping, drains, kerbs, steps, wet patches.
**The height** to the work and the size of the area to be reached: a single point, or a 30 m run of wall.
**The space**: obstructions such as racking, machines, counters and vehicles; doorways and ceiling height for a tower.
**The people**: shoppers, staff, pupils, patients, traffic; when the area is quietest.
**The hazards**: overhead lines, live boards and busbars, hidden cables, fragile roofs, chemicals, noise.
**The task**: how long it will take, what tools and materials must go up, how heavy they are, and whether two people are needed at the top.

head: Access
Best for
Limits
rows: Stepladder or leaning ladder
Short, light tasks of a few minutes where three points of contact can be kept, such as a quick check

No platform, no guardrails, nowhere to put tools; not for long jobs, heavy items or both hands overhead. Fibreglass near electricity, never aluminium. A leaning ladder stands at 1 out for every 4 up (about 75°), tied or footed.
Podium step or low platform
Short work at low height, such as changing a fitting on a 2.7 m ceiling
Low reach; a guarded platform on a small base.
Mobile tower (aluminium)
Work lasting hours or days at up to several metres, on a good floor, that must move along a wall or ceiling
Needs a firm, level floor and room to move; a height limit set by the base width; never near overhead lines; wind limits outdoors.
Fixed tube-and-fitting or frame scaffold
High, long or heavy work; poor ground; busy areas; outside walls
Built by scaffolders; needs ties to the building, more time and space.
Mobile elevating work platform (MEWP): scissor lift or boom
High or awkward work where a machine can be driven in
Only for trained, authorised operators; its own rescue and harness rules.

blocks.note: Chairs, tables, drums, pallets, stacked blocks and the top cap of a stepladder are not access equipment. A fall from 2 m onto concrete can kill.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: The risk assessment and method statement

blocks.p: The **risk assessment** lists the hazards of the job at height and the controls. The **method statement** says, step by step, how the access will be erected, inspected, used, moved and taken down, by whom, with what, and what happens if the weather changes or someone falls. Together they are the plan the team is briefed from. Include: the equipment and the maker's instructions; the trained erectors; the exclusion zone below; how materials go up (hand-line, gin wheel, never carried up the ladder); the electrical isolation needed; the weather limits; the **rescue plan**; and who inspects and tags.

head: Part
What it is
What it does
rows: Sole board (sole plate)
A timber or board laid on the ground
Spreads the load over soft ground so the scaffold does not sink
Base plate
A flat steel plate with a spigot, under each standard
Carries the standard's load onto the sole board; an adjustable (screw-jack) base plate lets the scaffold be levelled
Standard
An upright tube
Carries the load down to the ground
Ledger
A horizontal tube running the length of the scaffold, fixed to the standards
Joins the standards and carries the transoms
Transom
A horizontal tube across the scaffold, from front to back, resting on the ledgers
Carries the boards; a **putlog** is a transom with one end built into a wall
Brace
A diagonal tube
Stops the scaffold swaying and keeps it square: **ledger braces** across the width, **facade (sway) braces** along the face
Tie
A tube or anchor joining the scaffold to the building
Stops it falling towards or away from the building; removed only as the scaffold comes down
Lift
A level of ledgers and transoms
The working platforms are set at lifts
Bay
The space between two pairs of standards along the length
Scaffolds are described by their bays and lifts
Boards (decking)
Timber or metal planks on the transoms
The working platform
Guardrails
A **top rail** at about 1 m and a **mid rail** about halfway
Stop people falling from the platform edge
Toe board
A board on edge along the platform edge, about 150 mm high
Stops tools and materials being kicked off
Ladder or stair
Access to the platform, inside or in its own bay
The only way up and down

head: Coupler
Joins
Note
rows: Right-angle (double) coupler
Two tubes at 90°: standard to ledger
A load-bearing coupler
Swivel coupler
Two tubes at any angle: braces
Used for diagonals
Putlog (single) coupler
A transom to a ledger
Not load-bearing in the same way; never for standard-to-ledger joints
Sleeve coupler
Two tubes end to end, in line
An external sleeve; a **joint pin** (spigot) fits inside the tubes and is weaker
Base plate
A standard to its sole board
Fixed to the sole board where the rules say

blocks.p: A **frame scaffold** is built from ready-made welded frames (uprights and cross-pieces in one piece) joined with cross braces, pins and locks. A **system (modular) scaffold** uses standards with fixed connection points at set spacings. Both go up faster than tube and fitting and need less skill to assemble, but the maker's instructions must be followed exactly, and only the maker's matching parts may be used.

head: Part
Job
rows: Castors with brakes
Let the tower be moved; the brake on **every** castor is locked before anyone climbs
Adjustable legs
Level the tower on an uneven floor
Frames (end frames with built-in rungs)
The uprights and rungs; frames fit on each other by spigots and are locked
Horizontal and diagonal braces
Hook onto the frames and keep the tower square and rigid
Outriggers (stabilisers)
Widen the base so the tower cannot tip; the maker's instructions say when they are required
Platforms with trapdoors
The working deck; the trapdoor lets you climb through from inside
Guardrail frames and toe boards
Edge protection on the platform
The maker's instruction manual
The build order, height limits, loads, wind limits and outrigger rules for that tower

flow: Read the maker's instructions for this tower
Work out the allowed height and whether outriggers are needed
Barrier the area; check the floor and look up for hazards
Lay out and check every part
Build the base: castors locked, legs adjusted, level
Add frames and braces in the maker's order, checking level and square
Fit each platform, then its guardrails from a safe position, before standing on it
Fit toe boards on the working platform
Competent person inspects, records and tags

blocks.p: A freestanding tower can tip over if it is too tall for its base. Makers give a **height-to-base ratio** for their towers: commonly up to **3 to 1 outdoors** and **3.5 to 1 indoors**, measured to the platform, using the narrowest side of the base (outriggers count once they are fitted). Example: a tower whose narrowest base side is 1.8 m may go to 1.8 × 3 = 5.4 m platform height outdoors, and 1.8 × 3.5 = 6.3 m indoors. Above that, outriggers or a larger base are needed, or the tower must be tied. **Always use the maker's figures for the tower you have**; this is the common practice, not a rule for every tower.

head: Part
Reject if
rows: Tubes and frames
Bent, dented, cracked, split, heavily corroded, with damaged or distorted ends or spigots
Couplers
Damaged threads, bent or missing bolts, cracked or distorted bodies
Braces
Bent, or hooks and locking clips that do not work
Boards
Split, cracked, decayed, warped, burnt, paint-covered (which hides damage), knots that weaken them, metal end bands missing or loose
Platforms
Damaged decking, trapdoor or locks that do not hold
Castors
Brakes that do not lock, wheels damaged, missing or seized
Base plates and sole boards
Bent plates, rotten or split timber

blocks.p: The dangerous moment in building a tower is when a person is on a new platform with no guardrails yet. Two ways avoid it:

ul: **Advance guardrail system**: a guardrail frame is pushed up and locked in place from the level below, so the new platform already has rails before anyone steps onto it.
**Through-the-trap (3T) method**: the worker climbs up through the trapdoor, stays sitting in the opening with their body below the platform, and fits the guardrails from there before standing up.
Build it **level and plumb from the first lift**: a small lean at the bottom becomes a large one at the top and weakens every joint.
Fit that level's braces and guardrails **before anyone climbs higher**.
Climb inside, on the built-in rungs or ladder, **never up the outside** of the frames.
Lock every frame and brace with its clip or pin; use only the maker's parts.
Never use a tower as a support for a ladder, and never put a ladder, box or steps on the platform to gain height.
Pass parts up by hand from level to level, or use a hand-line; never throw them.

blocks.p: On soft ground, sole boards go down first, then base plates. Standards are set out with the ledgers and transoms level, and braced and tied as the scaffold rises. Couplers are tightened properly and never left loose for 'later'. Boards are laid close together, supported on enough transoms as the scaffold's design says, and **not overhanging** their end supports by more than a few times the board's thickness (a common figure is no more than four times the thickness, and at least 50 mm), so that a board cannot tip when it is stepped on. Erecting these scaffolds is scaffolders' work; your part is to know what a good one looks like.

head: When
By whom
rows: After it is erected, before first use
A competent person, recorded and tagged
At regular intervals during use (commonly every 7 days on sites, or as the site rules say)
A competent person, recorded
After any alteration, after strong wind or heavy rain, after any damage or event that could affect it
A competent person, before it is used again
Every day before climbing, and after any move of a tower
The users, with a quick check

ul: **Base**: firm ground, sole boards and base plates in place, castors locked, legs adjusted, outriggers fitted where required.
**Structure**: standards plumb, ledgers level, braces and ties all in place, couplers and locks tight, no damaged parts.
**Platform**: boards sound, close together, fully supported, not overhanging; trapdoors closed.
**Edge protection**: top rail, mid rail and toe board on every open side where a person could fall.
**Access**: ladder secure, inside the tower; no climbing route up the outside.
**Loads**: within the safe working load; materials tidy; nothing stacked against the rails.
**Surroundings**: exclusion zone below, no overhead lines close, no changes since the last check.

head: Tag
Meaning
rows: **Green** (with the date and the inspector's name)
Inspected and safe to use. Check the date: an out-of-date tag means the inspection is overdue.
**Red**: 'Do not use'
Not safe: incomplete, being altered, failed an inspection or being dismantled. Nobody climbs it, whatever their trade.
No tag
Treat it as not inspected: do not use it until a competent person has checked and tagged it.

blocks.p: Only the competent person changes a tag. Each inspection is written in the **scaffold register**: the scaffold, the date, who inspected it, what was found and what was done. The register shows that the checks were made and lets faults be traced.

The maker gives a **safe working load (SWL)** for each platform and for the whole tower. Add up everything: people, tools, cable drums, fittings, conduit. Two workers at 90 kg each and 70 kg of tools and cable is 250 kg. A cable drum can weigh more than a person; large or heavy items go up one at a time, and only what is needed for the task is on the platform.

ul: Check it before you climb: tag in date, brakes locked, rails and toe boards on, nothing changed.
Climb inside, with both hands free: tools go up in a bag on a hand-line or in a tool belt.

**Never move a mobile tower with anyone on it, or with materials on the platform.** Move it only by pushing at the base, on a firm level floor, with the height reduced as the maker says, after looking up for overhead hazards.
Do not remove a guardrail or brace to pass something up or to reach further. Plan another way: lower the work piece, use a hand-line, move the tower.
Do not lean out, stand on the rails or over-reach: move the tower instead.
Keep the platform tidy; take tools down at breaks.
Stop and report anything that looks wrong. Anyone may stop the work.

blocks.note: If you find a guardrail missing, a brake off or a split board, do not 'work carefully round it'. Get off, red-tag it, and report it. The next person may not know.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Protecting people below and preventing falls

head: Control
How
rows: Exclusion zone
Barriers and signs round the base, wide enough to catch anything that falls or bounces; a ground person to keep people and vehicles out.
Timing
Work above shop aisles, checkouts, corridors and car parks at quiet times, agreed with the manager.
Toe boards
On every working platform, so nothing is kicked off.
Containment
Tools and fittings in bags, boxes or buckets on the platform; nothing loose on the boards; brick guards or netting where small items could fall.
Tool lanyards
Drills, spanners and screwdrivers tethered to the worker or the tower, so a dropped tool does not fall far.
Lifting materials
A hand-line or a gin wheel (pulley) for fittings and tray; never carried up the ladder or thrown up or down.
Hard hats
For everyone on the tower and in the zone.

ul: A full platform with top rail, mid rail and toe board wherever a person could fall is the first line of defence.
Access is by the inside ladder; nobody climbs the outside or stands on the rails.
Trapdoors are closed once you are through them.
Guardrails go on before anyone stands on a new level, and come off only when that level is being taken down.

blocks.p: A **harness** does not stop a fall; it limits how far you fall and catches you. It is used where the rules, the maker, the site or the method statement require it: on a MEWP, where edge protection cannot be fitted, or while some parts of a scaffold are being erected or dismantled. The **lanyard** (often with a shock absorber) is clipped to an **anchor point** rated for fall arrest, never to a guardrail unless the maker says that rail is designed for it.

head: Harness check before use
Reject if
rows: Webbing
Cuts, frays, burns, chemical damage, stretched or stiff
Stitching
Broken, pulled or worn
Buckles, D-rings and hooks
Bent, cracked, corroded, or gates that do not close and lock
Shock absorber
Deployed (the cover torn or the pack extended) after a fall
Label
Missing, unreadable or the inspection date passed

blocks.p: A person left hanging in a harness after a fall can lose consciousness within minutes as blood pools in the legs (**suspension trauma**), so a **rescue plan** with trained people and equipment must be ready **before** the work starts: who will do what, with what ladder, tower, MEWP or rescue kit, and how 110 is called. 'Call the fire brigade' is not a plan: the rescue must be quick.

Aluminium towers and steel tubes conduct. If any part touches an overhead line, or comes close enough for the current to jump the gap, everyone touching the scaffold can be killed. The same applies to a long tube, a length of conduit or a tray being passed up.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Overhead lines near the work

Find them before planning. Keep the tower, tubes and people well clear (at least 3 m from lines up to 50 kV is a common minimum; more for higher voltages). Where work must be close, the team leader asks **JPS** for advice first: the line may be covered, switched off or a safe distance set. Never move a tower under or near a line.
Long items
Carry tubes, conduit and tray flat and low, with two people, and pass them up away from the line side.
Boards, busbars and live equipment near the tower
Before any work on or near them: switch off, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester checked before and after. Only the instructor or an authorised person re-energises.
Hidden cables in ceilings and walls
Check the drawings and use a cable detector before drilling.
Power tools on the platform
Battery tools where possible; otherwise GFCI protection, with leads kept clear of the rungs and the floor route.
Lightning
Come down and clear the tower when thunder is near.

head: Condition
Effect
What the team leader does
rows: Heavy rain
Softens ground and washes out fill, so a base sinks and the scaffold leans; boards, rungs and couplers become slippery
Checks the base again before anyone climbs; stops work in heavy rain; has boards cleaned of mud
Wind
Can blow a tower over; sheeting, banners or tarpaulins act as a sail
Follows the maker's wind limit (many say stop work at about 7.5 m/s, a fresh breeze, and secure or dismantle at higher speeds); never sheets a tower; watches forecasts
Tropical storm or hurricane warning
Towers blow away; fixed scaffolds loaded with loose boards come apart
Takes towers down and stores them; has fixed scaffolds checked, tied and cleared of loose boards and materials
After any storm
Ties, ground and parts may have shifted
A competent person inspects before use
Sun and heat
Aluminium gets too hot to hold; workers tire and dehydrate
Gloves, water breaks, shade where possible, work early

blocks.note: Wind speeds are measured at the site, not guessed. A hand-held anemometer is cheap; a tower on an exposed roof or a coast is in far more wind than one in a town street.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Dismantling, storage and leading the team

flow: Plan it as carefully as the erection; trained people only
Barrier the area and turn the tag to 'Do not use'
Clear tools and materials off the platforms
Take it down from the top, in the reverse order of erection
Keep guardrails on each level until that level is being removed
Keep ties and braces until the parts above them are down
Lower every part by hand or on a hand-line; never throw
Check, sort and store the parts

ul: Removing ties or braces too early is a common cause of scaffolds collapsing during dismantling.
Workers on the scaffold stay inside the guardrails of the level below the one being removed.
Dropped parts injure people below and damage the parts: everything is handed down.
Long tubes and frames are carried by two people, watching for people and lines.
Check every part as it comes down (see 'Checking the parts'). Damaged parts are **labelled and quarantined** for repair or scrap, so they cannot be used by mistake.
Clean off mud and concrete; dry boards.
Sort by type and size, and store in racks **off the ground and under cover**: sun hardens and cracks boards and castor wheels, rain rots timber and corrodes steel.
Keep the maker's manual with the tower, and count the parts back in against the list; a tower with parts missing cannot be built correctly.
Hired equipment goes back checked and complete, with any damage reported.
Before the job: check that the erectors are trained and authorised, that the tower, harnesses and tools have been inspected, and that the maker's manual is on site.

Brief the team from the risk assessment and method statement: the job, who does what, the exclusion zone, the electrical hazards and the isolation, PPE, the weather limits, how materials go up, the rescue plan, and that anyone can stop the work.

During erection: watch that the maker's order is followed, the castors are locked and guardrails go on before anyone stands on a level. Stop a trainee who takes a rail off or climbs the outside, put it right, and plan a safe way.
Before use: have it inspected and tagged; check it each morning and after rain, wind or a move; record the checks.
During use: brakes locked, loads within the SWL, nobody on a moving tower, tools tethered, the zone kept.
At the end: supervise the dismantling and storage, and report any damage.

blocks.p: Hard hat, gloves and safety boots for everyone erecting, using or working below a scaffold. Safety glasses when drilling overhead. A harness where required. High-visibility clothing where there is traffic.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can say what working at height means and the order of control for it.
I can survey a job and choose between a ladder, a podium, a mobile tower, a fixed scaffold and a MEWP, with reasons.
I can say what goes into the risk assessment and method statement for work at height.
I can name the parts of a tube-and-fitting scaffold and a mobile tower and say what each does.
I can name the couplers and say which joints each is for.
I can check scaffold parts and reject damaged ones.
I can work out the allowed platform height from the maker's height-to-base ratio.
I can describe building a tower in the maker's order, level, with castors locked, outriggers fitted and guardrails put in from a safe position.
I can explain the advance guardrail and through-the-trap methods.
I can carry out a check before use and explain the inspections, the register and the tag colours.
I can add up platform loads and keep within the safe working load.
I can state the rules for using a tower, including never moving it with anyone on it.
I can protect people below with an exclusion zone, toe boards, containment, tool lanyards and a hand-line.
I can say when a harness is needed, check one, and explain why a rescue plan must be ready.
I can keep metal scaffolds clear of overhead lines, isolate near live equipment and find hidden cables.
I can manage rain, wind, heat and storm warnings on a job at height.
I can dismantle top down, lower parts by hand, check, quarantine and store them.
I can brief and supervise a team on a job at height and keep the records.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: 1 in 4 (about 75°)
The angle for a leaning ladder
About 1 m and about 0.5 m
Usual heights of the top rail and mid rail
About 150 mm
Usual minimum height of a toe board
3 : 1 outdoors, 3.5 : 1 indoors
Common height-to-base ratios for freestanding towers; use the maker's figures
At least 3 m
A common minimum clearance from overhead lines up to 50 kV; follow JPS
About 7.5 m/s
A wind speed at which many makers say to stop work on a tower
7 days
A common interval for inspections of a scaffold in use

terms: A guardrail fitted from the level below, before anyone steps onto the new platform.
A fixing rated for a harness lanyard or a scaffold tie.
The steel plate at the foot of a standard.
The space between two pairs of standards along a scaffold.
A diagonal tube that stops sway and keeps the scaffold square.
Someone with the training, knowledge and experience to inspect a scaffold and say whether it is safe.
A long diagonal brace across the face of a scaffold.
A scaffold built from ready-made welded frames.
The strap, often with a shock absorber, that joins a harness to its anchor.
A horizontal tube along the length of a scaffold, carrying the transoms.
One level of ledgers and transoms.
Mobile elevating work platform, such as a scissor lift or boom lift.
The written step-by-step plan for erecting, using and dismantling the access.
A leg fitted to a tower to widen its base.
The most a platform or tower may carry, given by the maker.
Timber under a base plate to spread the load on soft ground.
Harm from hanging still in a harness; the reason rescue must be quick.
Fitting guardrails while sitting in the platform trapdoor, below the new level.
A fixing that joins a scaffold to the building.
A board on edge at the platform's edge that stops things being kicked off.
A horizontal tube across a scaffold that carries the boards.

c1.title: Cable tray in a Yallahs packing house
c1.text: A fruit-packing house near Yallahs, St Thomas, needs 40 m of cable tray and new lights along one wall at 6.5 m. The concrete floor is level but has a drain channel along the wall. Packing continues during the day, with forklifts in the aisle. The company's aluminium tower has a narrowest base of 1.45 m, and its manual gives a height-to-base ratio of 3.5 to 1 indoors and 3 to 1 outdoors, with outriggers raising the base to 2.6 m. Trainee leader Dwight plans the job with the Centre's instructor, who is the trained erector.

c2.title: Floodlights at a Santa Cruz football field
c2.text: A community football field in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, is getting new LED floodlights on four poles. Trainee leader Kadeem's team is to use a mobile tower on the grass beside each pole. JPS distribution lines run along the road about 4 m from one of the poles. The ground is soft after a week of rain, and the forecast gives gusts over 50 km/h for the afternoon. The team has a hand-line, tool lanyards, barriers and the tower's manual.

c3.title: A tagged scaffold at a Port Maria clinic
c3.text: A fixed tube-and-fitting scaffold has been left up on the side of a health clinic in Port Maria, St Mary, by the builders. Trainee leader Alicia's team must fit an outdoor light and a camera from it. The tag at the ladder is green but dated 19 days ago. On the platform Alicia finds a board with a long split, a gap where a toe board is missing, and a ledger whose coupler is loose at one standard. A painter is already working from the scaffold.

c4.title: Supermarket lighting in Linstead
c4.text: Trainee leader Shanice's team is replacing fluorescent fittings with LED panels above the aisles of a supermarket in Linstead, St Catherine, from a mobile tower, during opening hours. The manager wants the aisles kept open. A trainee suggests pushing the tower to the next fitting with the second trainee still on the platform holding the tools, to save climbing down each time. Another trainee has started to unclip a guardrail to pass a 2.4 m panel up from the floor.

c5.title: Returning a tower after a Black River job
c5.text: After a two-week job at a fish-processing plant in Black River, St Elizabeth, trainee leader Omari's team dismantles a six-frame mobile tower. One trainee begins to remove the diagonal braces from the bottom level first 'to make the frames easier to lift off'. Another wants to drop the platforms over the side onto the grass. When the parts are down, Omari finds a frame with a bent spigot, two castors whose brakes slip, and a platform with a cracked trapdoor.

questions.q: What is the greatest platform height allowed for the tower without outriggers inside the packing house?
o: About 4.35 m
About 6.5 m
About 5.1 m
About 9.1 m
questions.why: Indoors the ratio is 3.5 to 1, and the narrowest base side is used: 1.45 × 3.5 = 5.08 m, about 5.1 m. That is below the 6.5 m work height, so this tower needs its outriggers (2.6 × 3.5 = 9.1 m) before it may go that high. 4.35 m is the outdoor limit.

questions.q: Which arrangement best protects the packers and forklift drivers while the tower is used?
o: A sign on the tower, and a loud shout before each bracket goes up
A barriered zone, a ground person, toe boards, and quiet-time working
Lifting the tray quickly, so that it is above head height sooner
Asking the packers to look up whenever they pass the tower
questions.why: People below are protected by keeping them out: barriers, a ground person to control forklifts, and timing agreed with the manager. Toe boards, containment and tool lanyards stop things falling in the first place. Signs and shouting do not stop a dropped spanner.

questions.q: How should the drain channel beside the wall be dealt with when the tower is positioned?
o: Set two castors in the channel so the tower sits closer to the wall
Keep every castor on the firm floor, on plates across the channel if needed
Pack bricks under the castors over the channel to make up the level there
Run the castors along the edge of the channel and lock the brakes
questions.why: A tower must stand on a firm, level surface with every castor supported. A castor in or on the edge of a channel, or on loose packing, can drop or slide and tip the tower. If the tower must span the channel, it stands on sound plates laid over it, as the method statement says.

questions.q: What should Kadeem do about the pole that is 4 m from the JPS lines?
o: Use the tower there, since 4 m is beyond the 3 m minimum distance
Use a wooden ladder at that pole, since wood does not conduct
Put the tower on the far side of the pole and work round it
Get JPS's advice before any tower or tube goes near that pole
questions.why: A tower is tall and the lines may be nearer to the top than to the base, tubes and floodlight arms are passed up, and the ground is soft, so a lean is likely. Where work must be close to lines, the team leader consults JPS first: the line may be covered or switched off, or a safe distance set. A wet wooden ladder conducts.

questions.q: The grass is soft after the rain. What should be done before the tower goes up?
o: Set the castors on boards or plates and recheck the level
Push the castors firmly into the soft turf so that the tower cannot roll
Build the tower on its side and tip it upright when it is complete
Soften the castor wheels so that they grip the grass better
questions.why: A soft base lets a castor sink, and the tower leans and can topple. Boards or plates under the castors spread the load; the tower is levelled with its adjustable legs and checked again after each shower. Sinking the castors into the ground does not stop sinking further.

questions.q: With gusts over 50 km/h forecast for the afternoon, what is the right decision for the tower work?
o: Continue, as the floodlight brackets will shelter the platform from gusts
Continue with two workers on top to hold the tower steady
Plan to stop before the wind rises; lower or dismantle the tower
Continue after draping a tarpaulin over the windward side
questions.why: 50 km/h is about 14 m/s, far above the roughly 7.5 m/s at which many makers say to stop work on a tower. Work is planned so that the tower is down or secured before the wind rises. Extra people on top raise the centre of gravity, and a tarpaulin turns the tower into a sail.

questions.q: The floodlight heads weigh 18 kg each. How should they get up to the platform?
o: Carried up the inside ladder by the strongest trainee
Thrown up to a worker leaning over the top rail
Raised on the hand-line, with the zone below kept clear
Carried up the outside of the frames, which gives the better footing
questions.why: Climbing needs both hands and three points of contact, so nothing heavy is carried up a ladder, inside or outside. Materials go up on a hand-line or gin wheel, with the area below kept clear. Throwing anything, and leaning over the rail to catch it, risks a fall and an injury below.

questions.q: The tag is green but dated 19 days ago. What does this mean for Alicia's team?
o: It is in date, because a green tag stays valid until it is turned red
It was safe 19 days ago; the painter's use since then proves it still is
The inspection is overdue; the scaffold must be re-inspected before use
The team may use it if they first check it from the ground themselves
questions.why: A green tag is valid only until the next inspection is due, commonly every 7 days on a scaffold in use and after wind or rain. An out-of-date tag means nobody competent has confirmed the scaffold is safe. A users' look from the ground does not replace that inspection.

questions.q: What should Alicia do about the split board, the missing toe board and the loose coupler?
o: Ask the painter to avoid the board and work from the sound end of the platform
Tighten the coupler, turn the board over, and start work
Report them at the end of the day, once the light is fitted
Stop the painter, red-tag the scaffold and report the faults for correction
questions.why: Each fault could cause a fall or a collapse, and the scaffold must not be used by anyone, from any trade, until a competent person has corrected the faults and re-inspected it. Turning a split board over does not restore its strength.

questions.q: The loose coupler joins the ledger to a standard. Which type of coupler should be there?
o: A right-angle coupler
A swivel (angle) coupler
A putlog (single) coupler
A sleeve (end) coupler
questions.why: A ledger-to-standard joint carries load and is at 90°, so it needs a right-angle coupler. Swivel couplers are for braces at other angles, putlog couplers fix transoms to ledgers, and sleeve couplers join tubes end to end.

questions.q: What should Shanice say to the trainee who wants to push the tower with someone on the platform?
o: Allow it at walking pace, with the brakes locked as soon as it stops
Allow it, provided the worker on top holds the rails with both hands
Allow it for short moves only, because the floor is smooth and level
Refuse: everyone and everything comes off before the tower is moved
questions.why: A moving tower can catch a wheel on a tile edge or a cable and tip, throwing a person off. It is moved only from the base, on a firm level floor, empty, with the height reduced if the maker says so, after a look for overhead hazards.

questions.q: A trainee is unclipping a guardrail to pass a 2.4 m panel up. What should happen?
o: Let him, provided the rail is clipped back as soon as the panel is up
Stop him, refit the rail, and send the panel up by line or trap
Let him, if the second trainee holds his belt firmly while the rail is off
Let him, because a panel is too long to fit through the trapdoor
questions.why: A guardrail is removed only when that level is being dismantled. While it is off, the worker is one slip from a fall. Plan a safe way: raise the panel on a hand-line, pass it up on edge through the trap, or use a tower with a larger platform.

questions.q: The manager asks whether the aisles can stay open under the tower. What is the best answer?
o: Yes, if staff warn customers to walk quickly under the tower
No: the area below is barriered, so work is done at quiet times
Yes, because LED panels are light and would not hurt anyone
Yes, if the trainees keep their tools in their pockets
questions.why: Shoppers cannot be protected by warnings. The zone below the tower must be closed with barriers and a ground person, so the work is planned aisle by aisle at the quietest times, agreed with the manager. A dropped drill or a 2.4 m panel can seriously injure.

questions.q: Why must Omari stop the trainee removing the bottom braces first?
o: Bottom braces are worth more and must come off last to keep them clean
The braces keep the frames square; without them the tower can rack
Braces are only removed by the maker's own service staff
The bottom braces are what carry the tower's weight to the ground
questions.why: Dismantling goes top down, in the reverse order of erection, and braces stay until the parts above them are off. A tower without its lower braces can rack sideways and collapse with people on it. The standards carry the weight; the braces keep the structure square.

questions.q: What should be done with the frame with the bent spigot, the slipping castors and the cracked trapdoor platform?
o: Label them, keep them apart and send them for repair or scrap
Straighten the spigot with a hammer and oil the castor brakes
Store them with the rest, with a note in the manual
Return them to the rack unmarked, since the tower is not needed soon
questions.why: Damaged parts must not be built into the next tower by mistake. They are labelled, quarantined and repaired by the maker's method or scrapped. Bending a spigot back weakens it, and brakes that slip cannot be trusted.

questions.q: How should the tower's parts be stored at the Centre until the next job?
o: In racks by type, under cover, off the ground, counted
Stacked outside beside the fence, where the truck can load them
In one pile in the store, so that they take up the least space
Standing against the wall of the yard, where the sun dries them
questions.why: Sun hardens and cracks castor wheels and boards, and rain corrodes and rots parts. Sorting and counting parts means the next tower can be built complete, in the maker's order, from sound parts.

questions.q: A worker is to fit guardrails on a new tower level using the through-the-trap method. Where is she while she fits them?
o: Standing on the new platform, leaning over its edge to reach the rail posts
Sitting in the trapdoor opening, with her body below the new platform
Standing on the top rung of the frame below, reaching over the platform
Hanging on the outside of the frame on a harness clipped to the top rail
questions.why: In the 3T method the worker climbs up through the trap and stays sitting in the opening, protected by the platform around her, while she fits the guardrails above. Only when the rails are in place does she stand up on the new level.

questions.q: A worker falls from a scaffold and is caught by his harness. Why must he be brought down within minutes, not left until an ambulance arrives?
o: The lanyard stretches and will lower him slowly to the ground in any case
Hanging still in a harness restricts blood flow and can kill
The scaffold will fail under the extra load of a hanging worker
He may undo the harness himself and fall if he is left for long
questions.why: Hanging motionless in the straps traps blood in the legs, and the person can lose consciousness and die within a short time, known as suspension trauma. That is why a rescue plan with trained people and equipment must be ready before work at height starts.

questions.q: A team leader must choose access for replacing one fitting on a 2.7 m ceiling in an office. Which choice is usually right?
o: Standing on the office desk under the fitting
A full mobile tower built to its maximum height
A podium step or low platform with a guardrail
The top cap of a stepladder, held by a colleague
questions.why: A short, low task needs a stable guarded platform that is quick to set up: a podium step. Desks and stepladder caps are not access equipment, and a tall tower is more than the job needs and takes longer to erect safely.

questions.q: A platform is rated at 275 kg. Two workers of 85 kg and 95 kg are on it with 40 kg of tools. Which extra item would put it over its rating?
o: A 10 kg box of fittings
A 60 kg cable drum
A 20 kg length of tray
A 5 kg tester and tool roll
questions.why: 85 + 95 + 40 = 220 kg, leaving 55 kg. A 60 kg drum takes the total to 280 kg, over the 275 kg limit. Heavy items go up one at a time and only when needed, and the load is added up before it goes on.
